title: RAG and EPR
lines: RAG and EPR asks why individually relevant sources can form a weak evidence set.
Its first half builds a practical understanding of retrieval and grounded generation.
The second develops Evidence Portfolio Retrieval as a testable research proposal.
The proposed change is to select complementary evidence for a specific scientific decision.
Readers can compare that idea with modern retrieval methods before accepting its claimed value.

title: Relevant together, weak together
lines: Several retrieved documents can be individually relevant while repeating almost the same evidence.
A less similar source might contain the counterexample that changes the decision.
The book uses scientific assessment to explain why the collection itself matters.
Similarity remains useful, but it cannot describe every property of a useful evidence set.
That distinction motivates the proposed shift from isolated rankings toward portfolios.

title: A portfolio has obligations
lines: An evidence portfolio is selected for a stated task under an explicit budget.
Its members may provide support, criticism, boundary conditions, or alternative explanations.
Coverage, source dependence, and unresolved gaps remain part of the assessment.
Modern retrieval already includes related methods, so the proposal needs strong comparative baselines.
The book treats improved downstream decisions as a hypothesis to test, not an established advantage.

title: Read the comparison
lines: Begin with the engineering account of indexing, retrieval, context construction, and evaluation.
Then examine where independently ranked results fall short for a scientific decision.
The portfolio chapters explain an alternative representation and the comparisons needed to evaluate it.
RAG and EPR connects practical retrieval knowledge with a clearly bounded research question.
Read it to decide when better evidence selection requires thinking about the set.
